claims.text: A two-phase coexistence approach can be integrated with interface pinning or the Z method and on-the-fly machine-learning potentials within a DFT framework.
The proposed approach will reduce the computational cost of predicting melting properties relative to full ab initio thermodynamic integration.
The proposed approach will maintain sufficient accuracy for melting temperature, entropy of fusion, enthalpy of fusion, and volume change at melting.
Both solid and liquid phases of a high-melting refractory material can be simulated within DFT near the melting point.

The proposed intervention replaces full thermodynamic integration via ab initio molecular dynamics with two-phase coexistence, enhanced sampling, and on-the-fly machine-learning potential corrections.
Solid–liquid coexistence can be stabilized in simulations performed near the material's melting point.
Enhanced sampling and machine-learning potential adjustments dynamically capture and refine the solid–liquid interface.
Establishing phase coexistence directly locates the melting point.
Phase coexistence enables extraction of thermodynamic melting data with reduced simulation time.
Enhanced sampling and on-the-fly corrections mitigate errors arising from limited sampling.
Enhanced sampling and on-the-fly corrections mitigate finite-system-size errors.
The proposed approach lowers computational burden relative to full-scale thermodynamic integration.
The predicted melting temperature, entropy and enthalpy of fusion, and volume change will closely agree with conventional ab initio free-energy results.
The proposed calculations will require only a fraction of the computational cost of conventional ab initio free-energy calculations.
The method is expected to apply primarily to high-melting refractory materials with clearly defined phase coexistence.
Complex melting behavior or systematic errors in interface properties or machine-learning corrections may limit the method's performance.
The magnitude of discrepancies introduced by the cost-saving method is not precisely known.
